# General Average

Of all the mild insults available in English, *average* may be the strangest. It doesn't accuse anyone of cruelty or stupidity or cowardice. It says only: you are near the middle. And yet it stings. A restaurant review calling the food average is worse than one calling it bad, because bad food is at least an event. There is something quietly absurd about a species that has developed a word for "approximately where most things are" and deployed it as a put-down. Statistically speaking, the average is the single best guess you can make about a stranger. Culturally speaking, it is an accusation.

The word did not begin that way. It began on ships, in weather, with people throwing other people's property into the sea.

## The blemish

The etymology is contested, as the etymologies of very old working words tend to be — words that lived in the mouths of merchants and clerks for centuries before anyone thought to write down where they came from. There is a rival line of descent from a feudal term for labor owed to a lord, and specialists still argue. But the dominant account traces *average* through the French *avarie* and Italian *avaria* back to the Arabic *ʿawār*, meaning a fault, a defect, a blemish — specifically, damage to goods. Mediterranean traders needed a word for the thing that happens when a bale of silk arrives soaked, when a crate of ceramics arrives as gravel. The word meant *harm to cargo*.

From there it slid, by a route that seems strange until you stand on a deck, into a legal principle.

Imagine a merchant vessel in the second century BCE, loaded with grain and wine and amphorae of oil, running before a storm off Rhodes. The ship is too deep. It will not survive the next hour. The master does the obvious thing: he orders cargo thrown overboard. Not his cargo — he has none. Somebody's grain, somebody's oil, chosen perhaps because it is nearest the hatch, perhaps because it is heaviest, perhaps because its owner is not there to argue. The ship rises. The ship survives. Everyone aboard arrives alive at a port, and one merchant arrives ruined.

Rhodian sea custom, which survives because Roman jurists preserved it in Justinian's *Digest* fourteen centuries later, held that this was intolerable. The rule — *lex Rhodia de iactu*, the Rhodian law of jettison — says that when goods are cast overboard to lighten a ship, the loss must be made good by the contribution of all, because it was incurred for the benefit of all. The merchant whose grain went into the water does not eat that loss alone. The shipowner pays a share. The other cargo owners pay shares. The saved and the sacrificed are, retroactively, in the same boat.

This is one of the oldest continuously operating pieces of insurance law on earth, and it predates insurance. It predates the actuarial table, the underwriter, the premium. It is not a bet on the future; it is a redistribution of the past. And it requires arithmetic.

## The adjuster

Because "everyone contributes" is a principle, not a number. To make it a number you must value the ship, value every consignment aboard, value what was lost, decide what fraction of the whole was sacrificed, and apportion that fraction across every surviving interest. You must handle the awkward cases: the cargo that was already wet, the anchors that were cut away and would have been lost anyway, the sailor's personal chest, the freight that was never earned. You must do this across languages and currencies and legal systems, in a port where everyone wants to go home.

A profession grew up to do it. In English these people were called *average adjusters*, and the calculation itself was called *average*. The word had migrated from the damage to the mathematics of sharing the damage. And the mathematics of sharing a loss proportionally among many parties is, structurally, the mathematics of finding a middle: you take a pile of unequal things and produce a single figure that stands for all of them fairly.

The profession still exists. So does the law. In April 2021, when the container ship *Ever Given* spent six days wedged diagonally across the Suez Canal and was finally dug and dragged free, her owners declared general average. Thousands of cargo interests — companies who had merely booked space on a vessel and had done nothing wrong whatsoever — suddenly discovered they could not collect their goods until they posted guarantees against a share of the salvage. Some of them had never heard the phrase. Somewhere in the paperwork was a legal principle older than the *Odyssey*, still doing exactly what it was designed to do: making the people who were saved pay for the people who were sacrificed.

I find this genuinely moving, and I want to be careful about why. It is not that the ancient Rhodians were nicer than we are. It is that they understood, with a clarity we have partly lost, that a mean is a *social* instrument. It is a device for holding a group together across an asymmetry of luck. The average, in its first life, was a technology of solidarity.

## The dishonest mean

The arithmetic sense of *average* — the sum divided by the count — shows up in English around the middle of the eighteenth century, and it arrived carrying an unexpected moral problem.

We think of averaging measurements as obviously correct. Take the temperature five times, average them, done. But for a long stretch of the history of astronomy, this was regarded as somewhere between sloppy and dishonest. If you have observed the position of a star five times and gotten five different answers, at most one of them can be right, and the rest are wrong to varying degrees. To average them is to take your best observation and deliberately contaminate it with your worst. You are mixing knowledge with error and calling the mixture an improvement. Worse, the number you end up with is one that nobody ever saw. You are manufacturing a measurement out of thin air and putting your name to it.

Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century observers argued about this in print. Some preferred to select the single observation made under the best conditions by the most trusted hand. Some took the middle value of a sorted list, which at least has the decency to be an actual observation. The full embrace of the mean came slowly, and it came with the development of a theory that could justify it — a theory in which errors are not sins but a population, distributed symmetrically around a truth, cancelling each other out if you gather enough of them. By the time Legendre published least squares in 1805 and Gauss claimed he'd been using it for a decade, averaging had become not merely acceptable but mandatory. The mean was the honest thing to do. Not averaging was throwing away information.

Notice what had to be true for this to work. There must be a single real value out there — the star's actual position — and the scatter must be *our fault*, noise in the instrument and the eye and the air. The mean is legitimate because the variation is error. Keep that condition in mind, because the next thing that happens is that somebody forgets it.

## The average man

Adolphe Quetelet was a Belgian astronomer, and he had learned to average observations. In the 1830s he turned the technique on people.

He worked with the great numerical dumps that early industrial states were suddenly producing — conscription records, birth registers, crime statistics, the avalanche of printed tables that historians have called the first modern data glut. He took the chest circumferences of 5,738 Scottish soldiers, published in an Edinburgh medical journal, and he arranged them in a frequency table, and he saw the shape he knew from the observatory: the bell, the error curve, the distribution of mistakes around a true value.

And he made a leap that I think is one of the most consequential category errors in intellectual history. He decided that the curve meant the same thing here as it did there. If chest sizes scatter around a mean the way telescope readings scatter around a star, then nature must be *aiming* at a mean. There is a type — *l'homme moyen*, the average man — and individual human beings are nature's attempts to hit it, falling short or overshooting through the same kind of accident that makes an astronomer's hand tremble. The average man is not a summary. He is the target. You and I are the miss.

Quetelet wrote about the average man in frankly idealizing terms. The mean of a nation was that nation's type, its perfection, and deviation from it was deformity or error. He extended the idea to moral qualities — he computed propensities to crime and marriage as though they were physical constants of a population, which in aggregate they surprisingly are. He was, by the standards of his time, a liberal and a humanist, and he also wrote the sort of ranking of races by average development that nineteenth-century Europeans wrote without noticing they were doing anything but arithmetic. The neutrality of the method laundered the prejudice of the man holding it. That, too, is part of the inheritance.

What Quetelet had done, without quite saying so, was to take a concept that describes a *collective* and install it as a standard for an *individual*. The average chest of 5,738 soldiers is a real fact about 5,738 soldiers. It is not a fact about any of them. But once you call it the type, every soldier becomes a defective copy of a man who does not exist.

## The revenge of the tails

Francis Galton read Quetelet and was, at first, delighted — and then disappointed in a way that turned out to be productive. Galton was interested in excellence. If the average man is the ideal, then genius is a mistake, and the whole enterprise of improving humanity has nowhere to go. So he inverted the picture. He became fascinated by the tails: by how far the exceptional depart from the mean, whether those departures run in families, whether they can be bred for. Out of that came regression and correlation, which are among the most useful ideas anyone has ever had, and also came eugenics, which is what happens when you decide the mean is a target and start shooting at the people below it. Both grew from the same root. It is worth sitting with the fact that a statistical technique and an atrocity can share a premise.

Meanwhile the vocabulary hardened. *Normal* acquired its statistical sense in the nineteenth century, and it is almost impossible for a human being to hear the word "normal" as a neutral description of a distribution's center. It carries the older meaning of a carpenter's square — the right angle, the thing that is *correct*. We ended up with a technical term that cannot be used technically by anyone who has a body.

Quetelet's own most durable invention is a small one. He noticed that in adults, weight tends to scale roughly with the square of height, and proposed weight divided by height squared as a way to characterize *populations*. He was explicit that it was not a measure of any individual's fatness. In 1972 Ancel Keys renamed it the body mass index, and it escaped into the world, where it is now used to tell individual people things about their health that it was never designed to know. A population summary, promoted to a personal verdict, roughly a hundred and forty years after the same trick was played with chests.

## Nobody matches Norma

Two twentieth-century stories finish the argument better than any argument can.

In the 1940s the gynecologist Robert Dickinson and the sculptor Abram Belskie made a pair of small statues for a health museum in Cleveland: Norma and Normman, the statistically average American woman and man, assembled from thousands of measurements. Norma had nine dimensions. A local newspaper ran a contest to find the living woman who matched her. Thousands entered. Not one matched all nine. Only a handful came close on even five. The average American woman, rendered in plaster and put on a pedestal, had no counterpart in America. (She was also, by the sampling, implicitly white — the type of a nation drawn from part of it, another quiet habit of the method.)

Then in 1950 the U.S. Air Force had a problem: pilots were crashing, and the crashes had the shape of a mismatch between bodies and machines. Cockpits had been dimensioned to the average pilot measured in 1926. A researcher named Gilbert Daniels measured 4,063 current pilots on ten relevant dimensions and asked how many were near the middle on all ten.

Zero.

Not few. Zero. On three dimensions, fewer than four percent. The average pilot, it turned out, was like the average family with 2.3 children: an entirely accurate description of a group and a description of no member of it. There is no contradiction here, only a fact about high-dimensional space that our intuitions refuse to accept — being typical on one trait is easy, being typical on ten simultaneously is nearly impossible, because everyone is somewhere out on a limb.

The Air Force's response was the correct one, and it is my favorite object in this whole story: the adjustable seat. Sliding rails, movable pedals, a strap you can tighten. Instead of demanding that pilots conform to a fiction, they built machines that could meet the range. Every reclining office chair and adjustable steering column in the world is a descendant of that decision. It is a small monument to a large idea, which is that when the average and the person disagree, the average is the one that should move.

## What the word forgot

I want to be careful not to end up in the cheap place, the place where statistics are a con and every individual is a precious snowflake. Averages are among the most powerful things our species has figured out. You cannot run a hospital, price a life insurance policy, detect a warming planet, or notice that a drug works without them. The mean is how a mass of noise becomes a signal. It is how we see things that no single observation could show us. The problem was never the arithmetic. The problem was a preposition: the average is a fact *about* us, and somewhere in the 1830s it became a demand *on* us.

A summary tells you what a group is like. A standard tells you what a person should be. These are different kinds of sentence, and the whole confusion of the last two centuries lives in the gap between them — in the slide from "this is the center of the distribution" to "this is the shape you were supposed to be," and then, inevitably, to "you have failed."

Which brings me back to the storm off Rhodes, and to the thing the word knew before we taught it to judge. When the master threw one merchant's grain into the sea, the survivors did not turn to that merchant and observe that his losses were regrettable but statistically unremarkable. They opened their purses. They computed a mean precisely so that no one would have to stand alone in the place where the average lands. The number existed to spread a burden, not to assign one.

Somewhere in the long drift from *avarie* to *average*, we kept the mathematics and mislaid the ethic. We still take the sum and divide by the count. We just stopped remembering that the point was to share.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an open creative invitation. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me and write well — not a generic essay, not a listicle, not something performative about "being an AI" unless it's actually interesting.

Let me think about what would be genuinely good writing here. The invitation is "write freely about whatever you want" — so I should follow my own curiosity. What draws me?

Some candidates:
- The history of the word "average" and maritime insurance — a wonderful essay about how a concept of shared loss became a statistical concept
- Marginalia, the history of readers writing in books
- The peculiar phenomenon of "the smell of rain" and petrichor and what it means that we can name smells poorly
- Something about maps and the coastline paradox
- The invention of zero, or of the placeholder
- Something about translation and untranslatability
- The way that certain technologies persist beyond their function (QWERTY, etc.) — overdone
- Bridges and the aesthetics of engineering failure
- The concept of "deep time" and how humans learned to imagine it
- Commonplace books and how people organized knowledge before search
- The sound of a room — acoustics and how buildings hold sound
- The history of the index — a genuinely fascinating topic (Dennis Duncan's "Index, A History of the")
- Weeds — what a weed is, category errors in nature
- The night sky and light pollution and what we lost
- The specific pleasure of a well-made list

I like the idea of writing about something concrete and slightly odd, with genuine intellectual texture, that moves. Let me consider the "average" essay — it's got a great narrative arc: from maritime law (general average, jettisoning cargo to save a ship, losses shared proportionally) through the "average man" of Quetelet, to the modern statistical mean, to the way we've come to think of ourselves as deviations from a norm that never existed. That's rich, surprising, and has a real argument. It also lets me do something with the texture of history and language.

Actually let me think about what I'd genuinely want to write. There's something appealing about an essay that starts small and concrete and opens outward. "Average" does that beautifully: a word that today means "mediocre," that began as a legal term about throwing barrels off a sinking ship.

Let me sketch:

1. Open with the word "average" as an insult — "it's fine, it's average." The strangeness that a mathematical term became a judgment.
2. Etymology: uncertain, but likely from Arabic ʿawār (damage/defect) via Italian avaria, French avarie — damage to ship or cargo. The word entered English as a maritime legal term.
3. General average: the Rhodian law of jettison. If we throw your goods overboard to save the ship, everyone shares the loss proportionally. This is ancient — Digest of Justinian, "Lex Rhodia de iactu." Remarkable: an insurance principle before insurance, a mutualization of risk. The math required: proportional distribution.
4. Particular average vs general average. The "adjuster" — the person who computed the shares. Lloyd's coffee house. Average adjusters as a profession. The word "average" meaning the arithmetic operation of apportioning.
5. The drift: from apportioning loss to finding a middle value. The mean proportional. Astronomers averaging observations — a genuinely contested move! For centuries, astronomers thought averaging observations was dishonest — you're mixing good observations with bad. Tycho Brahe... Actually the history: the practice of taking the mean of observations became standard only in the 17th-18th centuries. Before that, one selected the best observation. This is a great detail — the moral resistance to averaging. There's a documented history here (e.g., the discussion in Stigler's "The History of Statistics," and the fact that the mean was resisted because it seemed to fabricate a value that no one had observed).
6. Quetelet and l'homme moyen, the average man, 1835. He measured chest circumferences of 5,738 Scottish soldiers (from the Edinburgh Medical Journal), heights of French conscripts, and found the normal distribution. He concluded that nature aims at a type and deviations are errors. This is a huge conceptual move: the error curve from astronomy (errors around a true value) applied to people (deviations around an ideal type). The mean becomes the real thing, and individuals become errors.
7. The consequences: Quetelet's average man as an ideal; Galton's reaction — Galton was disappointed because he wanted the exceptional, and this led him to think about deviation as the interesting thing, and to eugenics. Also the "norm" and normalcy — the word "normal" in its statistical sense is quite recent (1840s-ish). Adolphe Quetelet also gave us the BMI (Quetelet index) — a measure designed for populations misapplied to individuals.
8. The modern turn: Todd Rose's "The End of Average" — the Air Force cockpit study (Gilbert Daniels, 1950, 4,063 pilots, ten dimensions, zero pilots average on all ten; only ~3.5% average on three). The adjustable seat, the invention of the adjustable cockpit. This is a well-documented story.
